Direct HitProject record · built 2026-09-18

Direct Hit

Battleships, fought from the bridge of a battleship. There is no chart on a screen: you stand on the Littorio with your own fleet in formation around you, lay that fleet out on a lit plotting table, call a target on the same table, and take the shot through a director sight. If the round finds something, the camera goes to it - the vessel you hit, taking that shell at the point along her hull where you actually hit her - and afterwards she stays on your horizon, burning. When they fire back, you are standing on the ship they are shooting at.

5Ships
21Scripts
7Checks
5Looks
19Commits
14Decisions

How the game got made

Pipeline

The rules were built and proven before anything was drawn, because everything visible is generated from one dictionary the rules hand over: which ship, how far along her hull, and whether she went down. If the cutscene ever disagrees with the board, the board is right.

  1. AskWhere the cutscenes come from, what to build it in, who the player plays against - put to Luqman before a line was written.01-idea.md, 06-decisions.md
  2. Rules firstThe board, the fleet and the computer gunner, proven with nothing drawn.scripts/board.gd, dev/checks/_rules.gd
  3. HullsFive models downloaded, measured, and corrected in a table rather than edited.scripts/ship_models.gd
  4. Stage itOcean, sky, camera, shell, fire and smoke - all generated from the result of the shot.scripts/cutscene.gd
  5. LookPhotographs at exact beats, read back and judged by eye.dev/looks/, dev/shots/
  6. CheckHeadless scenes that end in a verdict, including the leak a correct rule set cannot catch.dev/checks/
  7. Play and reviewLuqman plays and reports back; the notes record what was decided.log/, 06-decisions.md

Tools

Godot 4.7.2Engine. Everything is built in code, including the board and the cutscene, so every camera mark and explosion timing reads in one file.
GDScriptAll game logic, the rules apart from the staging.
SketchfabAll five hulls, CC Attribution, normalised at load by ship_models.gd.
sfx (Freesound)CC0 sound only, with every file's source recorded in assets/audio/freesound/SOURCES.md.
ffmpegOne conversion: this build of Godot has no FLAC importer and drops the file without saying so.
Knowledge baseThe project notes this page is built from, kept outside the repo.

What the player sees

Screens

Every screenshot on this page was taken by a scene that drives the game from outside and saves a frame, because the questions that matter here are visual ones. A ship sailing backwards has exactly the same bounding box as one sailing forwards.

Inside the wheelhouse

The player stands in an enclosed steel wheelhouse mounted where the Littorio's own bridge was: a deck underfoot, four bulkheads, a deckhead overhead, a band of windows forward and one each side, and the fittings a bridge actually has. It is all built in code, because a hull model bought for use at half a mile does not survive being stood in. What the bought hull provides is everything beyond the windows - the foredeck and the turrets - which is the distance it is good at. An earlier version put the player on an open platform on top of the ship, which read as standing on the roof.

The plotting table

A lit glass plot on the bridge, carrying the same chart the flat version of the game used - rendered into a viewport and used as the table's own surface, so one piece of code decides what a hit, a miss and a sunk ship look like. The fleet is laid out on it before the action and targets are called on it afterwards, so the player has already used the table once before it starts mattering.

The gun sight

The bearing ribbon is the piece that matters. The plot gives a square, the square gives a bearing, and the ribbon is how the guns get onto it - which is the job a director sight actually did. The first version of this screen laid a lit grid on the enemy's water instead; see the note in Methods for why that could never have worked.

Under way

Three things that separate a fleet action from a diorama, all added on 2026-09-18. Her guns train on the square you called - the Littorio is a bought model with her turrets welded on, so both forward turrets are cut out of the merged meshes at load time and hung on nodes that can rotate. Every ship leaves a wake, drawn as a strip of mesh displaced by the same Gerstner waves as the sea it lies on. And the wrecks on the horizon burn in proper columns; for three attempts they came out as dark balls, and the cause was particle turbulence, which carries particles along with it rather than merely shaking them.

The fleet

Five real vessels, pulled from Sketchfab under CC Attribution and normalised at load rather than edited. One unit is one metre, and at sixty metres to a grid square four of the five come out within a few per cent of their real lengths. These are the photographs that caught the submarine sailing stern-first, and later every one of them riding with her main deck under water.

The moment the whole game exists for

The cutscene

Not a clip. The sea, the ship, the shell and the fire are generated live from the shot that was just scored, which is the only way the vessel on screen can be the vessel you hit and the hole can be where you hit her. A clip cannot know either. Any click skips it.

A hit she survives about three and a half seconds

A hit that finishes her about seven and a half seconds

The same shot on the smallest hull the framing has to hold at a quarter the length

01-idea.md · 7 sections

Idea

The idea as Luqman put it

"A battleships game, but whenever a player gets a hit, a cutscene of realistic ships getting hit appears." (2026-09-17)

What it became, the same day

"I want this game to be fully 3D. I want the battleship game to be in a real battleship, the environment is like navy is going to war. We as a player is the one controlling where to shoot." (2026-09-17, a few hours after the first build)

The rules did not change. Everything above them did. There is no chart on a screen any longer: the player stands on the bridge of the Littorio with their own fleet in formation around them, lays that fleet out on a lit plotting table on the bridge, calls a target on the same table, then puts an eye to the director sight and lays the guns on the bearing it gives them.

Four answers shaped it, all his: plotting table and then gun sight rather than one or the other; fixed on the bridge, free to look around, rather than walking the ship; the enemy's shells landing on your own ship rather than being reported; and a full war scene around the fleet.

One thing fell out of those answers that was not planned: your fleet of five becomes the ships around you. You stand on the battleship; the carrier, cruiser, destroyer and submarine are your escorts, in company. So when the enemy finds one of your ships, you watch it happen from your own bridge rather than reading it off a chart.

What the first version was

The rules of Battleships are untouched — a 10x10 grid, a fleet of five, alternate shots, sink everything. Everything built on top of that serves one moment: the half second after a shot lands on something.

When it does, the board is replaced by open ocean. The vessel you found is there, under way, at the size she should be relative to the others. A shell arcives from off the bow, the hull takes it where you hit it, and fire and smoke come out of the hole. If that was her last square she rolls, settles and goes under while the camera stands off and watches.

The decision that shaped everything else

Four ways to make those clips were put to Luqman: render them in Blender, generate them with AI, use CC0 stock footage, or build them in the engine and play them live. He chose real time in-engine, which is the most demanding of the four and the only one that can be correct: a pre-rendered clip cannot know that you hit the carrier three squares back from the bow, so it can only ever show a generic explosion and hope.

Target users

SegmentNeedWhy they'd pick this
Anyone who already knows BattleshipsNo rules to learnThe rules are the ones they know; only the payoff is new
Two people with one laptopSomething to play togetherPass-the-device mode needs no second device and no network

Value / advantage

  • The cutscene is accurate, not decorative — it is driven by the same dictionary that scores the shot.
  • Five real, recognisable vessels rather than abstract blocks.
  • No network, no accounts, no second device.

Assumptions to validate

AssumptionHow to testStatus
The cutscene stays a reward and does not become an interruptionPlay a full match and count how often the skip is useduntested — needs Luqman at the keyboard
~3.5s for a hit and ~7.6s for a sinking are the right lengthsSame playtestuntested
The computer at ~51 shots a game is a fair opponentPlay itmeasured, not felt

02-planning.md · 3 sections

Planning

Scope of v1 (built 2026-09-17)

In:

  • 10x10 board, standard fleet of five (carrier 5, battleship 4, cruiser 3, submarine 3, destroyer 2), no touching rule — overlap forbidden, adjacency fine.
  • Manual placement with a turn key and a scatter button, or scatter the lot.
  • Two modes: against the computer, and pass-the-device for two people.
  • A real-time 3D cutscene on every hit, and a longer one on a sinking.
  • Sea, sky, sound.

Out, deliberately:

  • Online play. It needs the Supabase project that is already outstanding for auxetic-chess and bluff-show, and two people on one laptop is enough for v1.
  • Difficulty levels. There is one computer opponent and it plays properly.
  • Salvo, mines, aircraft and the other Battleships variants.
What is left
  1. A playtest. Nobody has played this with their hands. Every claim about how it feels — cutscene length, whether the skip gets used, whether the computer is fun to lose to — is unverified.
  2. An export. No macOS or Windows build yet. referee-for-fun's tools/build/make_dmg.sh is the pattern to copy.
  3. Polish caught in review but left alone: the debris read as dark dashes rather than torn metal, and there is no wake behind a moving ship.

The project record exists as of 2026-09-17 — docs/index.html, built by tools/docs/build_docs.py and published at ~/Documents/dev/docs-site/direct-hit/index.html (docs-site open). It has to be rebuilt to that same URL whenever anything about the game changes.

Risks

06-decisions.md · 14 sections

Decisions

D-001 — The cutscene is built in the engine and played live (2026-09-17)

Chosen by Luqman from four options put to him: render the clips in Blender, generate them with AI (OpenArt credits), use CC0 stock naval footage, or build them in the engine in real time.

Real time is the most demanding of the four and the only one that can be correct. A pre-rendered clip cannot know which of five vessels you hit, or where along her hull, so it can only ever show a generic explosion. Everything that makes the idea worth building — the right ship, the right hole, a sinking only when she actually sank — depends on the cutscene being generated from the result of the shot.

Cost: an ocean, a sky, a particle system and a camera rig had to be built, and the sea is 360k vertices. It is rendered only during a cutscene and behind the title screen.

D-002 — Godot 4, not the browser (2026-09-17)

Chosen by Luqman. His last four games went to the browser, which is far easier to share, but real-time 3D of this kind is where Godot earns its place. The cost is distribution: people will download a build rather than click a link.

D-003 — Both modes, computer and pass-the-device (2026-09-17)

Chosen by Luqman over either alone. Online play was offered and declined for v1; it would need the Supabase project still outstanding from auxetic-chess and bluff-show.

D-004 — The board hands the cutscene one dictionary, and nothing else

Board.fire() returns which ship, how far along her hull, whether she sank. That dictionary is the only thing the cutscene is told. The cutscene decides nothing; if it ever disagrees with the board, the board is right. This is what makes it possible to check the rules with nothing drawn and still trust what is drawn.

D-005 — Models are corrected in a table, not in the files

The five hulls are left exactly as downloaded, and the scale, heading and waterline corrections live in ShipModels.TABLE. Editing the .glb files would have meant redoing that work every time a model is swapped, and would have hidden the corrections inside binary assets where nobody could read them.

D-006 — The view stays with the player against the computer

An early version let the on-screen viewpoint follow whoever's turn it was, which is right for two people sharing a device and badly wrong against the computer: it put the computer's own fleet face up on the player's chart every time it took a turn. The viewpoint now follows the device only when the device actually changes hands. dev/checks/_flow.gd tests this specifically.

D-007 — The game is played from the bridge, not from a chart (2026-09-17)

Chosen by Luqman, hours after the first version was finished: "I want this game to be fully 3D... we as a player is the one controlling where to shoot."

Four questions were put to him before anything was rebuilt, and his answers set the shape: the target is chosen on a plotting table and the shot is taken through a gun sight (both, in sequence, rather than one); the player stands in one place on the bridge and looks around rather than walking the ship; the enemy's shells land on the player's own ship rather than being reported; and there is a full war going on around the fleet.

The rules engine did not change at all. That is the payoff for D-004: because the board hands over one dictionary and decides everything itself, the entire presentation could be replaced without touching a rule.

D-008 — One unit is one metre (2026-09-17)

The game was built at roughly three metres to the unit, which was invisible until the player had to stand on a deck. At that scale a person is 0.6 of a unit tall, a handrail is 0.05, and every piece of human-sized geometry is a fraction.

Changing it meant retuning the sea, the particles, the drafts and the camera marks. It was worth it twice over, because at sixty metres to a grid square the fleet also comes out at its real size: the four-square battleship is 240 m, which is the Littorio to within a metre, and the carrier, cruiser and submarine land within a few per cent of their real lengths.

D-009 — No grid is painted on the sea (2026-09-17)

The first version of the gun sight laid a lit ten-by-ten grid over the enemy's water. It could not work, and not for any reason that colour or brightness could fix: a flat plane six hundred metres across, seen from a bridge twenty-four metres up at a range of six kilometres, stands about a tenth of a degree tall. It collapsed into a single hairline above the horizon.

Which is exactly why real gunnery never worked that way. The plot is on a table, flat in front of the people reading it, and what reaches the guns is a bearing and a range. So the sight now carries a bearing ribbon and a designator, the plot stays on the table, and the sea carries only things that are really there: your own fall of shot, and the ships you have set on fire.

D-010 — Your fleet is the fleet around you (2026-09-17)

The five ships the player lays out are the five ships in company with them: the battleship they are standing on, and four escorts on station. Nothing in the rules required this - it was free, because the fleet already existed as data - and it turns the enemy's turn from a report into something the player watches happen to a ship they can see.

D-011 — The player stands inside an enclosed wheelhouse (2026-09-17)

Luqman's, after playing it: "I want the player POV is in the ship, not above the ship. Create a bridge interior design and put the player there."

The first bridge was an open platform with a bulwark round it. Everything on it was correct and it still read as standing on the roof of the superstructure rather than being aboard, because there was nothing overhead, nothing behind and no walls - only a floor and a railing.

The wheelhouse is built in code for the same reason everything else near the player is: a hull model bought for use at half a mile has no interior at all. The measurement that decides whether it works is how far back from the glass the player stands - a pace and a half, which is the difference between a room and a window pressed against your face.

D-012 — The sky is a photograph, not a shader (2026-09-18)

Luqman: "take the sky hdri and put in the game."

The procedural sky it replaced could make clouds but could not make light. An HDRI carries the whole sky's brightness, so the ambient on the ships, the reflections on the water and the sky the player is looking at all come from one image and cannot disagree. The wheelhouse interior in particular went from needing its own lamps to being lit by the sky through its windows.

What it costs: 20 MB, and a fixed time of day. What it removes: a hand-written sky shader nobody has to maintain, and the whole class of mistakes where the lighting and the backdrop are tuned separately and drift apart.

D-013 — The bought hull's turrets are cut out of it so they can train (2026-09-18)

The player stands thirty metres behind the Littorio's forward guns and looks straight down them. Guns welded fore-and-aft while the plot says thirty-four degrees to starboard say plainly that none of this is real, so the turrets had to move.

The model cannot help. It is a Sketchfab materialmerger export: ten meshes merged by material and named Object_2 to Object_11, with no node called anything like a turret and no bone to drive.

Three options were on the table. Build turrets in code and lay them over the bought ones - rejected, because the bought barrels stick out fifteen metres and no code gunhouse can hide them once it trains. Leave the turrets welded - rejected, because it is the one thing in the frame that the player is staring at. Or cut the turrets out of the merged meshes at load time, which is what was done.

The cut takes every triangle whose centre falls inside a measured box, moves it into a mesh of its own on a node that can rotate, and shortens the index array of the mesh it came from. Vertex arrays are handed on untouched, so there is no seam and no duplication: dev/checks/_fleet asserts that the hull plus its turrets has exactly as many triangles as the hull did before - 80,611 either way, which is the check that would catch a duplicated surface, and the only one that would, because a duplicate looks perfect until the turret trains and the copy stays behind.

The cost of the decision is that the boxes are measured against one specific model and are written down in turret.gd with the reasoning for every bound. If the Littorio is ever replaced, they have to be measured again - dev/probe/_cut.gd paints each merged mesh a different colour and photographs her, which is how they were found. cut_from returns an empty array rather than failing if the meshes are not the ones it expects, so a swapped model gives welded turrets rather than no ship.

D-014 — A wake is a strip of mesh, not a particle system (2026-09-18)

It was a particle system first, because a wake looks like what particles are for: churned water dispersing. It was replaced for two independent reasons.

Cost. Eight hundred and fifty alpha-blended quads up to eighty metres across, with depth writing off so that nothing could reject a fragment, took one set of screenshots from eleven seconds to over five minutes. Transparency has no early-z to save it.

Looks. At any emission rate cheap enough to ship, the patches read as separate blobs of suds rather than a continuous track - which is worse than no wake at all on a sea already speckled with whitecaps.

A strip is one draw call of about two hundred triangles, one layer of transparency deep, the same on every frame, and its shape is exactly the shape a wake has. The thing a strip cannot do is stay where it was made when the ship turns - and that is affordable here only because she never turns. She steams in a straight line at a constant speed for the whole game, and along that line a strip fixed to her stern and a track left in the water are the same picture. If the fleet ever manoeuvres, this decision has to be revisited.

Two details carry it. The foam pattern is scrolled astern at exactly the ship's speed, so it stands still in the water while the strip carrying it moves with her. And the strip is displaced by the same four Gerstner waves the sea is, out of a shared shader include, so it rides the swell instead of being cut in half by the first crest that rises above it.

04-methods.md · 34 sections

Methods

Normalising a downloaded hull

Five models from Sketchfab arrived in five different units and headings: the battleship 23 units long down X, the destroyer 0.16 down Z, the submarine 1476 down Z. Rather than editing the downloaded files — work that would have to be redone the moment one is replaced — each is left untouched and the corrections live in a table in scripts/ship_models.gd: which axis the hull runs along, whether its bow points the wrong way, and how far up the hull the sea sits.

Every ship is then rebuilt to CELL_LENGTH units per grid square, so a 5-square carrier really is two and a half times a 2-square destroyer, and a hit on segment 3 of 5 lands three squares back from the bow.

One unit is about three metres. Wave sizes, particle sizes and camera distances are all written in that scale.

Measuring a model that is not in the tree yet

Godot refuses to give a global transform to a node outside the scene tree: it prints an error and hands back the identity, which silently measures a nested model as though every part of it sat at the origin. A hull has to be measured before it is added to anything, so ShipModels.measure() walks the transforms by hand instead of asking for global_transform.

Photographing the work instead of describing it

Numbers cannot answer visual questions — a ship sailing backwards has exactly the same bounding box as one sailing forwards. dev/looks/ holds scenes that drive the game from outside and save PNGs into dev/shots/:

SceneWhat it answers
_hullsIs every hull the right size, the right way round, floating at the right depth?
_cutsceneWhat does a hit actually look like, beat by beat?
_screensEvery screen the player passes through, menu first

This caught the submarine sailing stern-first, the fireball detached from the hull, particles the size of the ship, and a camera that followed a sinking ship under the water.

Gerstner waves, and the two ways to get them wrong

The sea is four Gerstner waves stacked. Two mistakes were made and both are worth remembering:

  1. The horizontal push must be tied to the wave's own amplitude (steepness * amplitude), never to steepness / wavenumber. Divide by the wavenumber and a short wave gets a sideways push larger than its own height, the surface folds through itself, and calm water renders as broken glass.
  2. The shortest wave must stay several mesh quads wide. Below about three quads per wavelength the mesh cannot hold the shape and the sea becomes crumpled foil that crawls as the camera moves. This, not artistic preference, sets the floor on how short the waves may be.

Ocean swell also runs roughly sixty times longer than it is tall. The first set of waves was three times too steep and every shot looked like a gale.

Checking a game that cannot be played by a machine

Three suites in dev/checks/, each printing numbers and exiting non-zero on failure:

  • _rules — placement, shots, sinking, and 300 full computer games.
  • _flow — drives the real screens: does the battle screen come up, does the computer's fleet stay hidden, does the device change hands correctly?
  • _assets — does every model, sound and shader the game names actually load, and is every CC-BY hull still credited?

Run them:

cd ~/Desktop/project/game/direct-hit G=/Applications/Godot.app/Contents/MacOS/Godot $G --headless --path . res://dev/checks/_rules.tscn --quit-after 2000 $G --path . res://dev/checks/_flow.tscn --quit-after 3000 $G --headless --path . res://dev/checks/_assets.tscn --quit-after 1000

_flow needs a window because it builds real Control nodes.

Two traps this project fell into

A check that prints "all passed" while its own script is crashing. A GDScript runtime error prints and carries on; a whole section of the rules check did nothing for one run while the summary still claimed success. Checks now prove the thing they are testing can even be constructed before testing it.

Godot dropping a file without saying so. This build has no FLAC importer. A downloaded .flac was ignored at import, ResourceLoader.exists() returned false at runtime, and the game would simply have had no splash sound. The asset check exists to turn that silence into a failure; the file was converted to .wav with ffmpeg.

Almost everything below was invisible from the cutscene's distance and obvious the moment a player stood on a deck. That is the theme: the close view is a much harder test than the wide one, and it finds errors the wide one cannot.

Draft is a depth, not a fraction

Every ship rode with her main deck under water. The ships were sunk to a fraction of the model's total height, and a model's total height includes its masts - so a ship with tall masts was pushed down further than one without. It is now an absolute draft in metres, and the numbers are the real ships' drafts.

At cutscene range, eighty metres off her beam, this was undetectable. Standing on the bridge it is the first thing you see: the sea washing over your own foredeck.

Ships were sailing backwards

Hulls are built with the bow at x = 0 and the hull running aft up +X, so making way is -X. Both the cutscene and the bridge were translating +X. With no wake and no bow wave there was nothing to give it away.

A bulwark blocks more of your own ship the further back you stand

A bulwark is a solid wall half a metre below eye level. How much of your own deck you can see over it depends entirely on how close you stand: three metres back it cuts off everything below eight degrees, which is the entire foredeck; with your waist against it you can see down at nearly forty. The first bridge put the player in the middle of the platform and the ship disappeared. Anyone on a real bridge stands at the rail, and now so does the player.

Two sheets of water at the same height fight for the same pixels

The sea is a fine sheet near the camera and a still one out to the horizon. At exactly the same height they z-fight across kilometres of overlap and the sea breaks into drifting mottled patches that read as an oil slick. A metre apart is not enough either - the near sheet's troughs still dip through. Eight metres down, the step where they meet is two kilometres away and subtends a fifth of a degree.

The horizon sheet also has to be enormous. The sea here is flat, with no curvature to hide an edge behind, so at 24 km across its own edge showed as a bright line across the sky. At 120 km it sits within a fiftieth of a degree of eye level.

Ripple normal maps alias into weather

Fine ripple added to the normal is what stops a swell looking like moulded glass. Seen from a kilometre away it is a fraction of a pixel, and what comes back is not ripple but moire: broad warm and dark patches drifting over the sea where the minified normal happens to catch the sun. It has to be faded out hard with distance, and so does anything else that samples the same noise.

Wave troughs should not be black

Reaching the deep colour as early as crest -0.4 turned every trough near-black. From a bridge twenty-four metres up you are looking down at troughs rather than across at crests, so the sea came out as drifting black blotches.

Particles are culled against a box a few metres across

A GPUParticles3D is culled against a visibility_aabb that defaults to a few metres, whatever its particles actually do. A smoke column rising eight hundred metres therefore vanishes the moment that little box leaves the screen - which, for something on the horizon, is most of the time. Every emitter needs room.

A particle system also starts empty and takes its whole lifetime to fill, so a wreck that has been burning for an hour shows three small puffs unless it is given preprocess.

A SubViewport used as a texture must render ALWAYS

UPDATE_WHEN_VISIBLE only counts a SubViewport as visible when it is inside a SubViewportContainer. Used as the surface of a table in the world there is nothing to make it visible, so it never draws a frame and the table comes out blank.

Twice over: the Control inside it needs anchors, not a size. A Control handed a size and no anchors can be laid back out to nothing, and a chart with no size draws nothing at all - which looks exactly like a viewport that never rendered.

A Control inside a CanvasLayer has no anchors to obey

It keeps a size of zero forever unless told otherwise, and every measurement taken from that size lands in the top-left corner of the screen. The HUD's reticle was being drawn at half of nothing.

Say which camera is current

Whichever camera enters the tree first otherwise wins. A stray Camera3D left in a test scene will happily film empty water while everything else works perfectly, and the symptom - a scene that renders but contains nothing - looks like a much deeper problem than it is.

Photographs lag the state that produced them

Waiting for two frame_post_draw signals is not always enough: a camera moved this frame can still be photographed a frame behind. A set of pictures that disagreed with the angles recorded alongside them is what exposed it. Recording the camera's actual angles into the same run is the cheapest way to tell a wrong picture from a wrong camera.

Checks that call methods never touch the input path

Twenty-three flow checks were passing while the game could not be played at all. Every one of them drove the game by calling its methods, and not one went near the mouse mode, the click routing or the key bindings - so a full-screen panel that swallowed every click, and a pointer that was never captured, both sailed straight through.

Two of the three bugs Luqman found on first playing it were in that gap. The checks now assert that no full-screen panel has anything but MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE, that the pointer is genuinely captured once the battle starts, and that a ship can be laid up and down as well as across.

A Control that covers the screen swallows every click behind it. Its own children still receive theirs, which is what makes this so confusing to diagnose: the buttons work perfectly and the world beneath them is dead.

Apply the pointer state from the setter, not from the next mode change. Opening the battle set the camera mode first and turned mouse capture on afterwards, so the one call that would have grabbed the pointer ran while capture was still off. Nothing changed mode again, so the pointer was never captured and the guns could not be turned for the whole game.

How far back from the glass

The single measurement that decides whether a ship's bridge reads as a room. With the eye up against the window the opening fills the entire view and the interior might as well not exist; a pace and a half back and the mullions, the sill, the deckhead and the side walls all come into frame and hold the sea inside them - while the sill is still low enough, from that distance, to see your own foredeck underneath it. Same principle as the bulwark note above, in the other direction.

Clicking the middle of a board proves nothing

The plotting table's picking was wrong from the day it was built. pick() took the plot surface's Y axis as its normal, when a QuadMesh lies in its own XY plane and faces Z - so every click was intersected with a plane at right angles to the chart, and landed on the wrong square.

It survived every check, a headless run, three look scenes and two sessions of review, because every test clicked the centre of the board. The centre of the board comes back as the centre square whatever the maths is doing. The test that finds it is the one that clicks a square away from the middle and asserts that the square you get is the square you clicked - now a round trip, with cell_world_position() as the exact inverse of pick(), so the two have to agree.

Drive the game the way a person does

dev/checks/_play.gd synthesises real InputEventKey and InputEventMouseButton events and pushes them through Input.parse_input_event, so they travel the whole input system: focus, GUI hit-testing, mouse filters, unhandled input. It clicks the menu button, lays a ship on the plot, calls squares, presses SPACE to reach the sight and to fire, and measures the frame rate at the size the game actually runs at.

Every other check in the folder drives the game by calling its methods. All of them passed on a game that could not be played. A check that reaches inside cannot tell you whether anyone can reach it from outside.

Two things to know when writing one:

  • Injected mouse positions are in window coordinates, a Control's rect is in canvas coordinates. This project stretches a 1920x1080 canvas to fill the window, so the two differ by a scale factor and clicks synthesised in the wrong space land somewhere else entirely - which looks exactly like a button that does not work.
  • Let the camera arrive before clicking. Mode changes tween the head over half a second, and a click sent before it has arrived is a ray fired from somewhere the player never was.
A single-sided surface has a side

Tipping the plot towards the reader is +TILT; tipping it away is -TILT. At nine degrees the difference is invisible. At forty, the wrong sign shows the player the back of the quad, which culls to nothing - so the chart simply is not there, and what they see instead is the table's casing and legs.

A room sets a limit on how far back you can stand

To read a board square-on at a 62-degree field of view you need to stand about its own depth away from it. A wheelhouse is two and a half metres from deck to deckhead, so a two-and-a-half-metre plotting table cannot be read inside one: there is nowhere to put the reader, and the camera ends up pushed through a bulkhead. The table was made smaller rather than the room bigger.

A captured pointer needs a way out

Once the battle starts the bridge takes the mouse. With no pause and no quit that is a trap - the cursor is gone, nothing on screen says how to get it back, and the only way out is to kill the program. ESC now always reaches a pause screen, which frees the pointer and offers a way off the ship.

Aim the sun at the sun in the sky

A photographed sky has its own sun in it. Light the scene from anywhere else and the shadows on the ships fall one way while the sky says the light comes from another - a mistake nobody can name when they see it, and everybody can feel.

dev/checks/_sunangle.gd finds it: the brightest point in the panorama, turned from a place in the image into a direction in the world. For this HDRI that is 37.8 degrees above the horizon, which is a good sign on its own - the file is called kloofendal_38d.

Two things it taught, both of which cost a run each:

  • The mapping is a convention and it is easy to mirror. Godot samples a panorama with u = atan2(dir.x, -dir.z) / 2pi, measured from the edge of the image and with the z axis negated. Measuring from the middle instead flips the sky left for right, and the sun comes out on the wrong side of the ship with nothing to complain about.
  • "The brightest pixel" is not the sun. On a rendered frame the sun blows out to pure white across a whole disc, so the first pixel brighter than everything before it is the top-left corner of that disc. The check reported the sun in the corner of a picture pointed straight at it. It now averages the position of everything within a whisker of the peak.

The answer is not trusted on its own: the check points a camera down the direction it worked out and confirms the sun really is in the middle of the frame. The angle is then pinned in dev/checks/_assets.gd, so swapping the panorama without re-deriving it fails instead of going quietly wrong.

Generated art needs a pass by hand before it is an asset

Four images were made on OpenArt for the interface. Not one went in as it came back, and the corrections were all the same kind: a generator answers the brief and not the use.

  • The key art was asked for twice, in two styles, and judged in the menu rather than on its own. A poster and an oil painting; both were handsome alone, and only with the title and buttons over them was it clear the poster's bow crowded the text column while the oil left it clean. Composition beats style when the picture has to hold words.
  • "Seamless, no seams, no rivets" produced seams and rivets. The steel came back as panel plating and the brass as a ribbed strip with screws. Rather than re-roll, a clean region was cropped out of each - found by searching for the window with the least variation across both axes, because measuring only the columns happily returns a window with a horizontal seam through it.
  • The chart paper's fold creases met in a bright star at the middle. Charming on a chart, and under a ten-by-ten grid it reads as a lamp burning a hole through the board. Subtracting a heavily blurred copy removes everything at that scale and leaves the fibre grain and foxing worth keeping.
  • The button plate is composed here, not generated. A StyleBox can carry a texture or a border, not both, so the steel and a brass edge are baked into one nine-sliced image in four brightnesses.
A pale surface shows every light in the room

The plot became paper and immediately grew a soft white blob through its middle. It survived turning the table's own lamp down, and then removing that lamp entirely, because it was never that lamp: at a low roughness the sheet was holding a mirror image of the wheelhouse's deckhead lamp. Paper is rough - 0.92

  • and the blob went with it.

Also worth knowing: StandardMaterial3D has no specular in Godot 4. Setting it falls through a Godot 3 compatibility remap that fails and warns on every build. The property is metallic_specular.

Particle turbulence advects; it does not jitter

This one cost three attempts at the same effect. The wrecks' smoke columns read as dark balls on the horizon, and every plausible cause was checked and corrected first - the sideways gravity that was throwing the smoke four kilometres downwind, and the puffs that were being drawn two hundred and eighty metres across. Neither was the reason. The reason was one line: turbulence_enabled = true.

Godot's particle turbulence is not a small perturbation added to a particle's own motion. It is a noise velocity field that carries the particle along with it, and at any noise scale broad enough to look like weather, the field is broader than the whole effect. So every puff, however hard it was thrown upward, was swept back into the same slowly churning knot of air. A ball, reliably, whatever the velocities said.

The general lesson: turbulence is safe on a short-lived effect and ruinous on a long-lived one. The hit smoke lives six and a half seconds and is fine. A column living nineteen seconds is entirely at the mercy of the field.

The way it was finally found is the method worth keeping. Four copies of the effect were put side by side, seven hundred metres apart, at a known distance with a known lens, each with one thing changed: as written, no preprocess, no turbulence, and a fixed frame rate. One render answered it. Printing the material's properties had already confirmed that every number was exactly what the code asked for - so the bug could not be in the values, and had to be in what one of them meant.

A plume is an aspect ratio before it is anything else

Both the wreck columns and the escorts' funnel smoke failed the same way for the same second reason: the puffs were wider than the plume was tall. Twenty quads two hundred metres across, overlapping, are a ball however fast they are travelling - it does not matter what the particles do if the thing drawn is wider than the shape it is meant to make.

So both are now specified as a ratio, and checked as one. The wreck column climbs eight hundred metres and is a hundred and seventy wide; a funnel plume climbs ninety-six and is fifty-four wide. They need different scale curves for this reason and not for an artistic one: a ship under way is making smoke, not on fire, and giving her plume the inferno's curve made it as wide as it was tall.

Cutting a moving part out of a bought, merged mesh

A Sketchfab materialmerger export has no parts. Object_10 is not a piece of the ship, it is every piece that happened to share one texture - which for the Littorio means the whole of A turret, and B turret's three barrels, and both triple secondaries out at the ship's sides, while B turret's gunhouse is in Object_11 instead. A turret is therefore a list of boxes in named meshes, and the only way to get that list right is to look at it.

The method: paint each merged mesh a different colour and photograph her. dev/probe/_cut.gd does this, and it turned a morning of wrong inferences into one picture. Before that, a vertex profile had been read as showing one forward turret and a raised deckhouse running aft; the coloured render showed two superfiring turrets, and the "deckhouse" was the upper turret's barrels lying over the lower one's roof at fifteen to seventeen metres.

The cut itself: sort every triangle by where its centre falls, take it whole or leave it whole, and hand the vertex array on untouched while replacing only the index array. Nothing is copied, so there is no seam. It can be run twice over the same mesh, which it has to be when two turrets share one.

The check that matters is the triangle count. The hull plus its turrets must have exactly as many triangles as the hull did before the cut. That is the only assertion that catches a duplicated surface, because a duplicate looks perfect until the turret trains and the copy stays behind.

Two smaller traps. A box floor is what keeps the barbette - the armoured drum a turret stands in, which does not rotate on a real ship either - behind where it belongs. And two turrets that overlap in length and in beam can only be told apart by height: B superfires over A, so the only thing separating her barrels from A's roof is that they are half a metre above it.

Foam on a Gerstner sea has to be displaced by the same Gerstner sum

A flat strip laid on a two-metre swell at a constant height is cut in half by the first crest that rises above it, and the gap reads as the wake being interrupted rather than as the wake being in a sea. Raising it above every crest is not a fix either - it then floats over the troughs.

The fix is for the foam to be displaced by the same waves the water is. That means the wave function cannot live in the ocean shader: it moved to assets/shaders/gerstner.gdshaderinc, included by both, so the two cannot be given different seas by accident. The uniforms that scale it are passed from one named constant each - Seascape.WAVE_SCALE and WAVE_SPEED - and a check asserts that the wake was handed the same numbers as the sea, because that is the failure that would put the foam back on a different swell.

Two mechanical notes for anyone doing this. A #include is textual, so moving a function out of a shader and leaving the old copy behind gives "redefinition" rather than anything helpful - and a function parameter may not shadow a uniform, which is why sea_fade takes begins and ends rather than fade_start and fade_end.

Overdraw is the only cost a transparent effect has

Eight hundred and fifty alpha-blended quads, up to eighty metres across, two faces each, with depth_draw_mode disabled so that nothing could reject a fragment: one set of screenshots went from eleven seconds to over five minutes. Nothing was wrong with the code. Transparency has no early-z, so the only thing that bounds the cost is not asking for it.

The three knobs, in order of how much they gave back: fewer particles, smaller quads, and one face instead of two. cull_mode = CULL_BACK on foam that lies flat under a player who is always above it is free - the underside is fragments nobody will ever see, and on a transparent surface those are fragments nothing will reject.

A check must not carry its own copy of the number it is checking

The funnel plume check multiplied the quad size by a hard-coded 4.0, which was the top of the wreck column's scale curve. When the plume was given a gentler curve of its own, the check went on reporting the column's width for it and failed a plume that was now correct. It reads the curve now.

A Godot scene whose script will not parse never exits

This is worth knowing because of how it presents. A parse error in the script on a scene's root node means the script does not load, the scene comes up empty, and nothing ever calls get_tree().quit() - so a headless check does not fail, it runs for ever. Twenty minutes went into looking for an infinite loop that did not exist. The error itself was one line: instantiate() is typed Node, so anything read off it is an untyped Variant and := cannot infer from it.

When a check hangs with no output, suspect the script before the logic, and remember that Godot buffers stdout when it is piped, so silence is not evidence of where it got to. Writing progress to a file with an explicit flush is what finally showed that nothing had run at all.

Technique
  • Gerstner waves — the standard formulation where horizontal displacement is steepness x amplitude x cos(phase) and the normal is built from the summed k x amplitude terms. Getting this wrong folds the surface; see 04-methods.md.
  • Naval facts worth keeping straight: a warship's ensign flies at the stern, which is how each model's heading was confirmed from a photograph rather than from its bounding box.

log/ · 2 sessions

Session log

2026-09-18

Three things were on the open list from the rebuild, and Luqman picked all three: no wake behind the fleet, wrecks reading as smudges rather than columns, and turrets that do not traverse. This session did those and nothing else.

The starting picture is worth keeping in mind: from the wheelhouse you looked out at glassy water with no wake on it, two round brown blobs sitting on the horizon, and your own main armament locked fore and aft while the plot said thirty-four degrees to starboard.

The turrets

The hard one, and it took two wrong readings of the model before it came right.

The Littorio is a Sketchfab materialmerger export: ten meshes merged by material, named Object_2 to Object_11, no node called anything like a turret and no bone to drive. There is no way to rotate what the model gives you, so the turrets are cut out of it at load time - every triangle whose centre falls in a measured box is moved into a mesh of its own on a node that can rotate, and taken out of the mesh it came from.

The first reading of the geometry was wrong, and the way it was wrong is the lesson. A vertex profile down the hull showed a structure at x 56..80 and a narrow raised thing at 15..17 m running aft from x 70 into the superstructure. I read the first as the forward turret and the second as a deckhouse, and cut accordingly. The render showed one turret swinging and another, unmoved, with its barrels overhanging the first.

What fixed it was painting each merged mesh a different colour and photographing her. In one picture: two superfiring turrets, A entirely in Object_10, B's gunhouse in Object_11 with B's barrels in Object_10 - and the "deckhouse" was those barrels, lying over A's roof. Numbers had been read for an hour; a picture took a minute.

They train at six degrees a second, which is what the real ones did, and the swing out to the enemy's bearing takes the better part of ten seconds. The muzzle flash and the departing shell now hang on the turret rather than on the centre line, because a flash on the centre line while the barrels point thirty-four degrees off it would be worse than never having moved them.

The wake

Built twice. The first version was a particle system, because a wake looks like what particles are for, and it failed on both counts at once: eight hundred and fifty alpha-blended quads up to eighty metres across took a set of screenshots from eleven seconds to over five minutes, and at any rate cheap enough to ship the patches read as separate blobs of suds.

It is now a strip of mesh - about two hundred triangles, one draw call, one layer of transparency. That works only because she never turns, which is true here and worth writing down as a condition rather than an assumption.

Two details carry it. The foam pattern scrolls astern at exactly the ship's own speed, so it stands still in the water while the strip carrying it moves with her. And the strip is displaced by the same four Gerstner waves the sea is - the wave function moved into a shared shader include for this - so it rides the swell rather than being cut in half by the first crest that rises above it, which is precisely what the flat version did.

The wrecks, and the thing that had been wrong all along

The columns had failed twice before and failed a third time this session, after two real bugs had been fixed in them: a sideways gravity throwing the smoke four kilometres downwind, and puffs being drawn two hundred and eighty metres across. Both were genuinely wrong. Neither was the reason.

The reason was turbulence_enabled. Godot's particle turbulence is a noise velocity field that carries particles along with it, not a jitter added to their own motion, and at any noise scale broad enough to look like weather the field is broader than the effect - so every puff, however hard it was thrown upward, got swept back into one churning knot. A ball, reliably.

It was found by putting four variants side by side at a known distance with one thing changed in each. One render. The same flag was balling up the escorts. funnel smoke, which from the bridge is the smoke the player actually sees - the escorts are a kilometre off and the wrecks are three to nine - so that was fixed in the same pass, along with a drift that was pushing funnel smoke astern at sixty metres a second off a ship making seven.

What it cost and what it bought

Sixty new checks in dev/checks/_fleet, and a look scene dev/looks/_fleet that photographs the three things a check cannot judge - most usefully the turrets trained hard over, where a wrong pivot would slide a gunhouse off its barbette. The strongest single check is that the hull plus its turrets has exactly as many triangles as the hull did before the cut: 80,611 either way. It is the only assertion that would catch a duplicated surface, which looks perfect until the turret trains and the copy stays behind.

All five suites pass. The battle runs at 50 fps, against the 32-49 recorded yesterday - smaller smoke puffs cost less to draw than the old ones did.

Still open

Unchanged by this session: she has never been played by hand. That remains the only thing that matters. Also outstanding: no Windows export and no .dmg, and the escorts appear to sit one full hull-length astern of their intended stations - _build_escorts pushes each hull aft by half its length where the comment says it means to centre it on the station. Left alone deliberately, because it was not on the list.

2026-09-17

What Luqman asked for

"Create a new game project. I want a battleships game but whenever a player get a hit, a cutscene of realistic ships getting hit appear."

Three questions, three answers

Before anything was built he was asked where the clips should come from, what to build it in, and who the player plays against. He chose real-time 3D in the engine, Godot 4, and both computer and pass-the-device. The first of those decided the whole shape of the project — see D-001.

What got built

  • The rules engine first, checked with nothing drawn: placement, shots, sinking, and a computer gunner that hunts on a checkerboard and follows a line once it has two hits. 300 games all finish, averaging 51.7 shots. Random guessing takes about 96; a good human plays around 45.
  • Five hulls pulled from Sketchfab and normalised at load rather than edited.
  • The cutscene: Gerstner ocean, cloud sky, a shell that arcs in, fire, smoke, spray, debris, and a separate longer sinking.
  • The board: a drawn naval chart, fleet pips, placement with a turn key, two modes, and a handover screen.
  • Sound, all CC0.
  • Three check suites, all passing.

What went wrong, and what it taught

Almost every real bug was invisible in the code and only appeared in a photograph:

  • The submarine sailed stern-first. A bounding box cannot tell you which end is the bow; the propeller in a render can.
  • The fireball burned in mid-air beside the ship, because it was parented to the world instead of the hull.
  • Particles were the size of the ship — a particle's scale multiplies its quad, so a 6-unit quad at scale 16 is a 96-unit puff.
  • The camera followed a sinking ship under the water, because it was hanging off the hull. It now rides its own rig at sea level.
  • The sea rendered as broken glass, twice, for two different reasons — both now written up in 04-methods.md because both are easy to repeat.
  • A check printed "all passed" while its own script was crashing.
  • Godot silently dropped a downloaded FLAC; this build has no FLAC importer.

And one bug found by reading rather than looking: against the computer, the viewpoint followed whoever's turn it was, which would have shown the player the computer's entire fleet every time it fired. There is now a check for exactly that.

Where it stands

Playable end to end in both modes, all checks green — and never once played by hand. That is M6 and it is the next thing that matters. No export, no project record yet.

What Luqman asked for

"I want this game to be fully 3D. I want the battleship game to be in a real battleship, the environment is like navy is going to war. We as a player is the one controlling where to shoot."

Four questions, four answers

Asked before anything was rebuilt, because this replaced almost everything above the rules. He chose: the plotting table and then the gun sight, in sequence; fixed on the bridge, free to look around, rather than walking the ship; the enemy's shells landing on his own ship; and a full war scene around the fleet. See D-007.

What got built

  • The bridge of the Littorio: platform, bulwark, rail, compass, voice pipes, all built in code, because a hull model bought for use at half a mile does not survive being stood on. The bought hull provides the foredeck and turrets below and ahead, which is the distance it is good at.
  • A lit glass plotting table carrying the same chart the flat version used, rendered into a viewport and used as the table's surface, picked by intersecting the camera's ray with the table's own plane.
  • Laying the fleet out happens on that table too, so the player has already used it once before it starts mattering.
  • A director sight: bearing ribbon, elevation ladder, a designator on the sea, and a tolerance the guns have to be inside before they will fire.
  • Guns, a shell that arcs for two and a half seconds, and a fall of shot.
  • The enemy firing back onto the player's own fleet, with the bridge shaking by how close it landed.
  • The war: four escorts in company, funnel smoke, aircraft going over, gunfire on the horizon and burning wrecks.
  • The rules engine was not touched.

The scale changed

One unit is now one metre. At three metres to the unit a person is 0.6 of a unit tall and every handrail is a fraction, which stopped being workable the moment the player had to stand on a deck. Retuning the sea, the particles, the drafts and the camera marks took a while and was worth it twice: at sixty metres to a grid square the fleet also comes out at its real size.

What the close view found

Standing on a deck is a much harder test than watching from eighty metres away, and it found four things that had been wrong all along and invisible:

  • Every ship was riding with her main deck under water, because draft was a fraction of the model's total height and that includes the masts.
  • Every ship was sailing backwards.
  • The two sheets of ocean were z-fighting, which is what all those drifting mottled patches were.
  • Particle emitters were being culled against a visibility box a few metres across, so any smoke that rose properly simply vanished.

And one thing that was geometry rather than a bug: the gun sight's first design laid a lit grid on the enemy's water, and a flat plane six hundred metres across seen from twenty-four metres up at six kilometres is a tenth of a degree tall. It collapsed to a hairline. Which is why real gunnery keeps the plot on a table and sends the guns a bearing - so that is what the sight does now.

Where it stands

All three check suites pass, now twenty-three flow checks driving the real screens. Still never played by hand. The wrecks read as dark smudges rather than columns of smoke, there is no bow wave or wake behind a fleet that is now plainly under way, and the ship's own turrets do not traverse.

Luqman played it, which is the thing that had been missing all day, and came back with three things.

"I cannot go up and down to put the ship"

Ships could only be laid across the plot, not up and down. Two causes, both mine:

  • A full-screen panel was eating the clicks. The placement bar's holder is a Control stretched over the whole screen, and a Control that covers the screen swallows every click before it reaches the world behind it. Its buttons still worked, which is why this looked like "turning does not work" rather than "nothing works".
  • Turning her was on one key and nowhere else. It is now R or right click, and the instruction line says which way she is currently lying, because the ghost only appears once the pointer is over the plot - so with the pointer anywhere else there was no feedback at all.

"After I choose a box, I cannot attack"

The pointer was never captured, so turning the guns was impossible: the cursor hit the edge of the screen and the sight stopped.

The cause was one line in the wrong order. Opening the battle set the camera mode first and handed the bridge the mouse afterwards, so the single call that would have grabbed the pointer ran while capture was still switched off. The screen is now shown first, and setting capture_mouse applies the pointer state itself rather than waiting for the next mode change.

Both are now checked: one check asserts that no full-screen panel swallows clicks, another that a ship can be laid up and down and that the ghost really runs that way, and a third that the pointer is genuinely captured once the battle starts.

The lesson is about the checks, not the bugs. Twenty-three flow checks were passing while the game could not be played at all, because every one of them called methods directly and none of them went anywhere near the input path - the mouse mode, the click routing, the key bindings. Checks that drive a game from the inside will never find a game you cannot reach from the outside.

"I want the player POV in the ship, not above the ship"

Fair. The bridge was an open platform with a bulwark round it, which reads as standing on the roof of the superstructure rather than being aboard.

It is now an enclosed wheelhouse: ten metres across, five and a half deep, two and a half from deck to deckhead, with a band of windows forward and one each side, a doorway aft, dark corticene on the deck and two lamps under the deckhead. In it are the wheel, two engine telegraphs, the compass, voice pipes, a grab rail under the forward windows and the plotting table.

The one measurement that mattered was how far back from the glass the player stands. With your nose on it the opening fills the whole view and the wheelhouse might as well not be there. A pace and a half back and the mullions, the sill and the deckhead all come into view and hold the sea inside them, while the sill is still low enough to see your own foredeck underneath it.

Terse, and fair. He had played it twice and it had not worked either time.

The bug

The plotting table's picking, wrong since the day the table was built. pick() took the surface's Y axis as its normal; a QuadMesh lies in its own XY plane and faces Z. Every click was being intersected with a plane at right angles to the chart, so clicks landed on the wrong squares.

From the player's side that is exactly "I cannot go up and down to put the ship" and "after I choose a box, I cannot attack" - you click a square and something else happens, and there is no way to tell whether the game is broken or you are.

It survived everything, across two sessions, because every test clicked the middle of the board - and the middle of the board comes back as the middle square whatever the maths is doing.

The check that should have existed from the start

dev/checks/_play.gd drives the real game with synthesised keyboard and mouse events pushed through the whole input system, rather than by calling methods. It clicks the menu button, lays a ship, calls squares away from the centre and asserts each lands on the square that was clicked, reaches the sight, fires, and measures the frame rate at the size the game actually runs at.

Writing it found the bug in its first run, once it stopped clicking the middle.

Frame rate, while it was at it: 32-49 fps maximised on the retina screen. Not the problem, but not comfortable either.

Also done

  • The board faces the reader, as he asked: tipped up forty degrees and framed square-on along its own normal. Two things went wrong on the way - the first attempt tipped it away, which shows the back of a single-sided surface and therefore nothing; and the table was too big to be read inside a wheelhouse two and a half metres high, so the camera was pushed through a bulkhead. The table is smaller now.
  • ESC always reaches a pause screen that frees the pointer and offers a way off the ship. A captured pointer with no pause and no quit is a trap.
  • The prompts are legible: what to do next is on a dark strip at the bottom of the screen in readable type, instead of small grey text over the sky.
  • A macOS build, so it can be opened by double-clicking instead of typed as a command. Ad-hoc signed and launched to prove it starts.

What this session was really about

Two sessions of checks passed on a game nobody could play. The checks tested whether the machine was right; none of them tested whether a person could reach it. That gap is now closed, and the lesson is worth more than the bug.

dev/checks and dev/looks, from each scene's own header

Checks and looks

A check runs and ends in a verdict. A look takes screenshots for a person to judge. Both are scenes under res://dev/. Between them they caught a submarine sailing stern-first, a fireball burning in mid-air, particles bigger than the ship, a camera that followed a sinking vessel under the water, and the computer's own fleet appearing face up on the player's chart.

Checks
SceneWhat it asks
_assetsIs everything the game names actually there?
_fleetThe fleet: her guns, her wake, and the smoke around her.
_flowCan a whole match be played from the menu to the last ship, and does the bridge ever show something the player is not entitled to see?
_playCan the game be played with a keyboard and a mouse?
_rulesDoes a shot do what it says it does?
_shipsHow big is each hull, and which way is it pointing?
_sunangleWhere is the sun in the sky image, and does the game's sun agree with it?
Looks
SceneWhat it asks
_bridgeInside the wheelhouse, looking each way.
_cutscenePhotographs of a hit, beat by beat.
_fleetThe fleet under way: her guns, her wake and the wrecks on the horizon.
_hullsA parade of all five hulls, on real water, photographed from close by.
_screensEvery screen the player passes through, in order, menu first.
